posts: Two minutes is the whole design. If you stretch it to five because the conversation is going well, you have turned it into a chat, and it is the ten day run that does the actual work.

The para version exists because you rarely get a student on your own. Put your two minutes where you already stand, arrival, transitions, the walk to specials, instead of inventing a slot you cannot protect.
Which student would you pick if you had to start tomorrow, and what is making you hesitate about that particular one?
Paras, does your lead teacher know when you are running something like this, or is it easier to do it quietly and say nothing?
Stations go out before students arrive, not while they wait. The checklist puts that first because a queue at the paint trolley is where most of the mess actually begins.
The reset list is written to be handed over. If a student can read it and run it, you get your last five minutes back instead of spending them alone at the sink.
Which material causes the most chaos in your room, and have you found a station layout that calms that one down?
How do you handle the student who finishes early and appoints themselves in charge of cleaning everyone else's table?
Three moves, not ten, because the week back is not the week for a new system. Re-teach one routine, rebuild one relationship habit, and leave everything else where it is.
The part aimed at the adult is not filler. Coming back tired and pretending otherwise is what turns a rough Monday into a rough fortnight.
Which break is hardest to come back from where you are, winter, spring or a long weekend, and what makes that one worse than the others?
What is the first routine you re-teach afterwards, and do you announce it or just quietly run it again?
The five areas stay scored separately on purpose. A beautifully set up room and a teacher running on four hours of sleep is not a ready classroom, and a single score would hide that.
Self-care sits in the same list as materials because it is a readiness condition, not a reward handed out for surviving September.
Which of the five did you score lowest on, and was it the one you expected before you started scoring?
If you were handed one free afternoon before students arrived, what would you spend it on, and would that have been the same answer five years ago?
This audits conditions, not personality. Warmth is not a condition. Whether a wrong answer costs a student anything in front of peers is.
Run it around week six rather than week one. Culture in the first days is mostly novelty, and you would be auditing a room that no longer exists by October.
Which condition came out weakest for you, and what would have to change in the room itself before it shifted?
How do you tell the difference between a quiet class that feels safe and a quiet class that has simply gone silent?
Choose three routines to open with, not the whole pack. Systems fail when eight are taught at once and none of them ever get properly practised.
The procedures here are written as sequences you teach rather than rules you post. That difference is the entire reason some stick and others just live on a wall.
Which routine in your room saves you the most time, and how long before it ran without you standing over it?
For anyone in their first couple of years, which system did nobody warn you that you needed until the week it fell over?
Colour is doing the work in most of these. Give each colour one meaning and keep it all year, otherwise you are handing out pretty rectangles and calling it a check.
Foldables take longer the first time than anyone expects. Build one yourself before asking thirty people to follow the folds, or the lesson disappears into origami.
What happens to the offcuts where you are, saved in a tub or straight in the bin, and has anyone found a use worth the storage?
Has anyone found a way to store construction paper that survives a full year, or does every system end as a bent stack on a cupboard?
Sticky notes work on an anchor chart because they can be moved and thrown away. A chart written in marker is finished, and students stop touching finished things.
Gallery walks fall apart at the reading stage. Give people something to do with what they read, sort it, challenge it, add to it, or they walk, look and remember nothing.
When students post on a gallery walk, do you keep it anonymous or ask for names, and what changed when you switched?
Where do anchor charts go once a unit ends, rolled up somewhere hopeful or straight in the recycling, and do students ever ask for one back?
Written for rooms where the furniture is not up for discussion. If your desks move, this is the wrong tool and a layout guide will serve you better.
Partner work in rows holds together if you fix who turns to whom before the task starts. Left shoulder, right shoulder, decided in advance, so no minute is lost to negotiation.
For anyone teaching in a lab or lecture room with bolted seating, what movement have you genuinely got working in that space?
Has anyone argued their way into different furniture, and what did that take, a work order, a sympathetic caretaker, or three years of asking?
Chalk is slow, and the slowness is usable. Whatever you write stays up for as long as you keep writing, so this board suits building one idea across a lesson rather than flashing six.
Contrast is the accessibility problem here. Thin white chalk on a worn green board is unreadable from the back, so press harder and write larger than feels necessary.
For anyone still teaching on a chalkboard, is that by choice or because the building never replaced it, and would you swap if you could?
What actually gets a blackboard properly clean rather than grey, and how often does it need doing before the back row can read it?
Silent discussion is the underrated one on this list. Nobody interrupts anybody, slow processors get equal air, and the whole conversation is still standing there to read afterwards.
Give the board up. The moment students may write on it without asking, it stops being your announcement space and becomes a working surface.
Do students in your room write on the board without asking, and if not, what has stopped you handing it over?
For anyone who has tried silent board discussion, how did you bring in the students who write nothing and wait it out?
Sort student work before you touch a single cupboard. That is the pile with decisions in it, and left until the last day it all goes into the recycling unread.
Leave a note for whoever has this room next, even if you are certain it is you. Plans change over the summer and a labelled cupboard is a kindness.
What do you always regret throwing out, and what is the thing you keep hauling to the next room and never use?
Does your building give you timetabled time for this, or does the packing up happen on your own hours after everyone else has gone?
Split by day rather than one long list, because the order is the point. Relationships, then procedures, then content, and the first week is the only chance you get to set that sequence.
Do not finish the room before students arrive. Leaving wall space empty means what goes up is theirs, and the space starts belonging to them straight away.
What do you always run out of time for in the first week, and have you ever managed to move it earlier?
For anyone starting in a new building this year, what would you most want to know by the Wednesday?

Setup is access before it is decoration. A clear path to the door, a seat that works for a wheelchair or a walker, and somewhere to go when the room is too much, all of that comes before display boards.
Representation on the walls counts only if it outlasts September. A heritage display that comes down in October tells students exactly how permanent they are in this room.
What is one change to your room that turned out to help far more students than the one you made it for?
How do you set up a calm space that students actually use, rather than one that becomes a place they are sent and learn to avoid?

Serial numbers at the point of issue, not in June. A checklist filled in from memory at the end of the year is a guess, and a guess is what turns a missing instrument into one person's word against another's.
Condition notes earn their keep more than counts do. Knowing a case latch is broken in October is what stops it becoming a cracked body by March.
Music teachers, who actually pays when a school owned instrument comes back damaged, the family, the department, or nobody at all?
How often do you run a full check, termly or once a year, and has that frequency turned out to be enough?
Teach the rotation with nothing at the stations first. Five and six year olds can learn the movement or the task, not both, and sloppy movement costs you a fortnight.
The signal matters more than the timer. Choose one sound and never change it, because the day you improvise a new one the whole room stops rotating and starts watching you.
How many stations do you run before a K-2 room stops being manageable, and does that number change with how many adults are in it?
For the other adults in the room during rotations, do you stay at one station or move along with a group?
Work through it before students are in the room. Checking eyewash and goggles with thirty people already at the benches means checking under pressure, and that is how a gap gets waved through.
The emergency section is the one people skim because nothing has ever happened. Knowing where the shower and the cut-off are matters only in the ten seconds you will not have to look them up.
Who checks the eyewash and shower in your building, and how do you know when it was last actually done?
What is your rule for the student who turns up to a practical in open shoes, and does the building back you if you sit them out?
Shadow boards or numbered slots, so a missing tool is visible rather than discovered. A count at the end of a session tells you something has gone, not when or with whom.
Five minutes means the timer goes at five minutes, not when a build looks finished. The routine only holds if it starts at the same point every session regardless of what is half done.
Which tool keeps walking out of your space, and has anything actually stopped it, signing out, shadow boards, or just knowing who to ask?
How do you handle students who want to keep working while everyone else packs away, do builds stay out or is everything cleared every session?
The introduction script is in there because nobody hands paras one. Saying out loud what you do and what you need takes half a minute and saves a term of guessing on both sides.
Ask about the hard things in week one while asking is still normal. Behaviour plans, personal care, who to call, what you may decide alone. By week six those same questions sound like complaints.
Paras, what is the one thing you wish you had asked your lead teacher on day one instead of working it out the hard way in October?
For teachers, what do you genuinely want a new para to ask you, rather than quietly work out on their own?
Every station goes out before the first group walks in, including the one you will not reach until the third rotation. Building a station while a class waits is where the lesson leaks.
Transition cues have to carry across a full gym. A whistle pattern or a hand signal that reads at distance beats a spoken instruction nobody at the far wall will hear.
How do you run stations when the gym is shared with another class, do you split the space or split the time?
What do you do with the group that finishes a station in half the time you planned, hold them there or give the station a second layer?

Teardown is the part with no adrenaline left in it, which is precisely why it gets rushed. The order here is waste, then glassware, then surfaces, so nothing hot or sharp is handled once attention has gone.
Waste disposal is not a student job unless your building says so in writing. Build the routine around what students may legitimately handle and keep the rest with you.
How many minutes do you protect for teardown, and is that ring-fenced or the first thing to go when a practical runs long?
When more than one class shares a lab, how do you leave it for the next teacher, and what do you expect to find when you walk in?
Consumables and reusables are counted separately for a reason. One tells you what to order, the other tells you what to repair, and a single combined number gives you neither.
Audit at the end of a unit rather than the start of one. You will still remember what broke, and the order goes in early enough to arrive before you need it again.
Who holds the budget for kit replacement where you are, and how far ahead do you have to ask for it?
Has anyone found a way to stop kits coming back to the cupboard incomplete, without becoming the person who checks every box?
Language sits in this audit next to the furniture because it is part of the room. Whose names get said properly, whose home language is allowed through the door, that is setup too.
Do this one alongside another person. The parts of a room you have stopped seeing are exactly the parts an audit you run alone will miss.
Which section of the audit was uncomfortable to sit with, and did anything in the room actually change as a result of it?
Whose work is on your walls right now, and if you are honest about how those pieces got chosen, what does the pattern say?
Repeatable is the whole design. Ten minutes students can predict beats ten brilliant minutes they cannot, because the predictable version still works on the day you walk in unprepared.
Admin belongs inside the ten minutes rather than before them. Register, notices, chasing a missing book, all of it running underneath something students are already doing.
What does your first ten minutes look like right now, and did you design it or did it just happen to you?
For anyone who changed their opening routine mid-year, how long did it take before students stopped pushing back on it?
Naming the levels is what stops the nagging. Once silent, partner and group each mean something specific, you are pointing at a level rather than telling someone off.
Name the level before the task, never during it. Announcing a volume after the room has already got loud is correction wearing the costume of a system.
What do you do when the level is right for the task but still too much for one particular student in the room?
Does a named volume system survive in spaces that are loud by design, gyms, workshops, music rooms, or do you need something else entirely there?
Design once, teach well, is the actual claim being made. Most procedures that fail were never badly designed, they were explained in September and never practised again.
Write each one as steps a student could follow with you out of the room. If a step needs your judgement, it is not a procedure yet, it is a decision you are still making.
Which procedure did you have to rebuild partway through the year, and what was it that broke it?
How many procedures can a class hold before students stop tracking them, and do you drop some deliberately or let the weak ones fade?

Visual management means the board answers the questions students would otherwise bring to you. What are we doing, how long have I got, what happens when I finish, all readable without a hand going up.
Keep the layout in the same place every single day. The value is a student orienting in two seconds from a glance, and that only happens while the zones stay put.
What has earned permanent space on your board, what gets wiped every lesson, and has anything moved between those two?
In multilingual rooms, how much of the board ends up in more than one language, and who decides which parts?
Say what you are about to do before you do it, every time, including with a student who cannot answer you. Dignity and consent are not conditional on being able to say yes out loud.

Learn the plan and your building's rules on who may be present before you are ever in the situation, not during it. Written expectations protect the student first and you second, and both of those matter.
For paras supporting older students, how do you keep this private when the timetable makes it obvious where someone is going?
What does a good handover look like when personal care is shared between more than one adult, and how do you spare the student explaining themselves twice?
This one is about your voice, not the students'. A para prompting from across the room carries much further than it feels, and it competes with the teacher instead of supporting them.
Move closer rather than louder. Almost every volume problem in a support role is solved by crossing the room, which also keeps the redirection between the two of you instead of public.
Paras, has a teacher ever told you that you were too loud, and how was that raised with you at the time?
What signal do you and your lead teacher use when one of you needs to hand the room over to the other?
